source.title: Toto 2.0: Time Series Forecasting Enters the Scaling Era
source.authors: E. Khwaja; C. Lettieri; Gerald Woo; Eden Belouadah; Marc Cenac; G. Jarry; Enguerrand Paquin; Xun-Yi Zhao; V. Zhukov; Othmane Abou-Amal; Cheng-Hao Liu; A. Talwalkar; David Asker

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates forecast quality across time-series model sizes, extending scaling research to a different modeling domain. It does not test language-model pretraining loss or fit power laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports forecast benchmark results across Toto 2.0 sizes. These bear on V6's scale-versus-task-performance relationship, but not on language-model cross-entropy, power-law fits or extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture sensitivity, or the same power-law form in another modality. Hyperparameter-search results are not scaling-law measurements. The finetuned and ensemble leaderboard results are explicitly not used to support the zero-shot scaling claim and are not included.
record.test_reason: This study trains five time-series forecasting models (4m to 2.5B) and reports benchmark ranks by size. It fits no power law and measures no language-model loss. It does not relate downstream scores to LM scale or pretraining loss. V6 concerns downstream tasks of language models, so these rows do not measure what V6 names. V5 needs the same power-law form in another modality, and five benchmark ranks with no fit cannot show a form. The size sweep is also confounded: the 4m and 22m saw 3.40T points over 400k steps, the larger three 5.04T over 600.5k steps. CRPS rank is relative to the comparison pool, not an absolute loss. The paper invokes Kaplan et al. as motivation, so it discusses rather than tests the claim. The size-quality trend is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors claim a single recipe gives reliable, smooth forecast-quality gains from 4m to 2.5B on BOOM, GIFT-Eval and TIME, with only minor inversions on TIME rank metrics. They call this a 'GPT-2 moment' for time-series models. They fit no scaling law and report no loss-vs-scale curve.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales time-series forecasting models and evaluates forecast benchmarks; it does not use the language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law measurement or fit described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark changes the observed scaling pattern: the authors report a non-monotonic comparison between 313m and 1B on TIME rank metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: Under one u-µP-transferred recipe, Toto 2.0 forecast quality improves with size from 4m to 2.5B on BOOM and GIFT-Eval. On TIME, 313m edges out 1B on both rank metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Time-series foundation models trained under a single hyperparameter-transferred recipe improve monotonically (mostly) in zero-shot forecast quality with parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger sizes keep coherent structure further past the training context on synthetic multi-scale signals (Pearson r by size and horizon, Figure 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Long-horizon forecast stability of time-series foundation models increases with model size.

record.problems: The reported outcomes are forecasting benchmark ranks, not held-out pretraining loss or fitted power laws. The text provides no uncertainty estimates for these scaling comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Other benchmark metrics (including CRPS, MASE, and their ranks) are shown in Figures 5, 6 and 8 but are not separately catalogued here; this record selects CRPS rank as the stated primary ranking measure for the size trend. Finetuned and ensemble results in Section 5.3 are excluded because the authors state they are not used to support the zero-shot scaling claim.

untested.parts: No LM held-out loss and no power-law fit in N, D or C.
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation; tokens differ by size class only incidentally.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count. Proxy architecture sweeps tune components, not depth/width at fixed N.
Time-series modality, but no power-law form fitted or tested; only five sizes reported as ranks.
No LM downstream tasks; no relation of performance to pretraining loss or a fitted scale trend.
No exponents or fitting choices examined.

missing.what: Absolute CRPS and MASE values per Toto 2.0 size on BOOM, GIFT-Eval and TIME. These would be needed to check any power-law form in this modality.
Pearson r vs ground truth per size at 2,048/4,096/8,192-step horizons.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link is rejected: V6 concerns LM downstream tasks, and rank-on-benchmark for a time-series model is a different system and measure. Ranks depend on the external model pool. Size is confounded with training data (3.40T vs 5.04T) and steps (400k vs 600.5k). No uncertainty is reported. The finetuned/ensemble results were correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship is measured.
No power law is fitted on smaller runs or used to predict larger runs.
No loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is evaluated across compute budgets.
The study does not compare depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates time-series models at different sizes, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in this or another modality or training regime.
No relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance is evaluated; results concern forecasting benchmark scores versus model size.
The study does not assess fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor test for departures from a power law.

relation.reason: The introduction invokes language-model scaling and cites Kaplan et al.; the study's own results concern forecasting quality rather than testing or applying a fitted scaling law.

tranche.reason: The study reports forecast-benchmark improvements across model sizes, but tests no power-law form, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or quantitative downstream scaling prediction. The size sweep alone does not establish a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Model size changes alongside architecture and training budget: 4m/22m receive 3.40T points and 400,000 steps; larger models receive 5.04T points and 600,500 steps. TIME has a stated 313m-over-1B rank inversion.
